title: Twin-beam advantage in quantum LiDAR under correlated noise
abstract: Quantum light promises improved precision in optical remote sensing, but its practical advantage depends critically on whether nonclassical resources remain useful under realistic noise and experimentally accessible detection. This question becomes especially relevant for LiDAR systems, where a quantum advantage has been demonstrated for target detection and joint range-velocity estimation, but mostly under idealized conditions or simple noise models, such as optical loss and thermal background. A key open point is whether entanglement provides an operational advantage when the dominant disturbance is not independent noise, but structured interference across sensing modes. Here, we address this question by studying the joint estimation of target range and velocity with bright two-mode Gaussian probes and homodyne detection, comparing coherent, separable squeezed, and twin-beam states at a fixed resource budget. Our results reveal a hierarchy of quantum resources set by the noise structure: separable squeezing provides a robust advantage over coherent illumination under loss and thermal background, whereas twin-beam probes become superior under correlated jamming when the receiver is adaptively optimized. These results establish correlated noise as the operational regime in which entanglement provides a robustness advantage beyond local squeezing, opening a receiver-aware route to quantum-enhanced LiDAR in realistic and potentially adversarial environments.
summary: This work analyzes quantum LiDAR performance to determine when entanglement offers an advantage over simple squeezing under realistic noise. By modeling correlated jamming noise, the authors show that twin-beam states provide superior estimation precision compared to classical or locally squeezed light. This establishes a receiver-aware protocol for achieving practical quantum enhancement in remote sensing.
main_problem: The study investigates whether entanglement provides a genuine operational advantage over local squeezing for quantum LiDAR when the dominant noise source is structured, correlated interference rather than independent noise.
main_result: Correlated noise establishes an operational regime where twin-beam probes outperform both classical and separable squeezed states, provided the receiver adaptively optimizes its measurement basis.
method: The analysis uses a unified Gaussian framework to compare three quantum probe types (coherent, separable squeezed, twin-beam) by calculating joint estimation performance metrics like Fisher Information and Mean Square Error for range and velocity estimation.
model_or_system: The system is a Quantum LiDAR setup performing joint range ($	au$) and velocity ($\omega$) estimation using bright two-mode Gaussian probes detected via homodyne measurements. The noise model incorporates both standard loss/thermal background and structured correlated jamming noise.
key_observables: Joint range–velocity estimation performance (variance products), Mean Square Error (MSE) of parameter estimates, and the ratio quantifying the advantage between different quantum states.
important_parameters: Fixed total signal energy ($N=50$), correlated noise strength ($\sigma_c$), and the adaptive optimization of receiver measurement settings (LO phases).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the receiver can adaptively optimize its measurement basis to maximize accessible information, moving beyond simple theoretical bounds.
figures_summary: Figures compare joint estimation performance vs. correlated noise strength ($\sigma_c$), showing the hierarchy of advantages; other figures detail reconstruction MSE and covariance ellipses for different probe types under varying conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general problem in quantum sensing to modeling specific noise regimes (loss/thermal vs. correlated jamming). It then compares the performance metrics across coherent, separable squeezed, and twin-beam states, culminating in demonstrating the operational advantage of entanglement under structured noise via simulation.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, experimentally relevant roadmap for achieving quantum enhancement in remote sensing by identifying the specific noise structure (correlated interference) that unlocks the full potential of multipartite entanglement over local resources.
